entities.name: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party – Syria Region
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Arab Socialist Baath Party – Syria Region, the Syrian branch of the pan-Arab Baath Party, has ruled Syria continuously since the March 8 Revolution (1963) — making it one of the world's longest-ruling single parties — first through a series of military coups and party factions, then under Hafez al-Assad's consolidated personal dictatorship (1970-2000), and now under Bashar al-Assad whose mishandling of the 2011 Arab Spring protests triggered a civil war that has killed over 500,000 people and displaced 13 million.

The Syrian Baath Party's rule has been defined by the Assad family dynasty (Hafez and Bashar), the dominant role of the Alawite minority (Assad's sect) in the security services, and a brutal suppression of opposition exemplified by the 1982 Hama massacre (killing 10,000-40,000 Muslim Brotherhood supporters in the city of Hama). The Baath Party's pan-Arab socialist ideology — which promised unity, freedom, and socialism — was progressively hollowed out, serving as ideological veneer for Assad family rule and Alawite sectarian dominance.

The 2011 Syrian uprising — part of the Arab Spring — began as peaceful protests responding to the torture of children and rapidly escalated into civil war as Assad's government responded with mass arrests, torture, and military force. The conflict drew in ISIS, Al-Qaeda affiliates, Kurdish militias, Turkey, Russia, Iran, the US, and other powers, creating one of the most complex multi-actor wars of the 21st century. The Baath Party's decisions in 2011 — to crush rather than reform — produced one of the largest humanitarian disasters since World War II.
